title: Way Out West

subtitle.text: Howdy! Long ago lots of folks wanted a new life.
So they headed way out west.
This story is about two of them.
Their tale begins in a crowded city.
"Thief!" a mink shouted.
"You stole my pearl necklace!"
The thief was a cat named Cleo.
She darted down the street, smiling.
But as she turned a corner, that smile disappeared.
Roscoe was blocking her path.
That dog was the toughest cop in town.
"You're under arrest, Cleo."
"No way, Roscoe!" Cleo yelled and ran the other way.
She looked back.
Roscoe was behind her.
Cleo ran faster.
She turned a corner and slipped through an alley.
"Whew!" Cleo said. "I lost him!"
She turned down another alley.
She ran past some barrels and stopped.
"Oops! This is a dead end!"
Cleo spun around and gulped.
"Roscoe!"
"You're trapped, Cleo," the dog said.
Cleo sighed and handed over the necklace.
"You caught me.
But I'll have better luck next time."
"There won't be a next time," Roscoe said.
"You're going to jail."
Cleo's shoulders slumped.
Roscoe smiled. "And I'm catching the next train out west."
That was a surprise.
"West?" Cleo said.
Roscoe nodded. "A little town called Prickly Pear needs a sheriff.
Maybe I'll get some peace and quiet for a change."
"When are you leaving?" Cleo asked.
"Now," Roscoe said.
"I was on my way to the train station.
But then I saw you steal the necklace."
He grabbed her paw.
"Let's go. The train leaves soon. I don't have much time."
They walked to the police station.
Cleo saw his train ticket and had a sneaky idea.
As they passed an apple cart, Cleo grabbed an apple.
She tossed it in the air.
It landed on Roscoe's hat.
The apple seller frowned. "You have to pay for that!"
"Huh?" Roscoe said.
"You have one of my apples," the seller said.
"He's right," Cleo said. "It's on your hat."
"How did it get up there?" Roscoe said.
As Roscoe reached up, Cleo grabbed his train ticket.
Then she ran fast.
At the train station, a whistle blew.
"The train!" Cleo thought.
"It's leaving the station!"
Cleo hopped on and gave her ticket to the conductor.
She sat down and let out a long breath. "Whew!"
Then she heard a shout.
Out the window she saw Roscoe.
The poor dog was trying to catch the train!
Cleo laughed as the train sped up.
She was headed west.
Cleo woke to the sound of a train whistle.
The train rocked gently as it chugged along.
Outside she saw dirt, rocks, and cacti.
Cleo smiled. "I'm not in the city anymore."
The train stopped.
"End of the line, folks," the conductor said.
"Prickly Pear!"
Cleo followed other passengers off the train.
She reached into her pocket and pulled out two coins.
"Two coins won't buy much," Cleo thought.
She looked around, wondering what she could steal.
But nobody was wearing a pearl necklace—or any other jewelry.
Soon the other passengers were gone.
A tumbleweed rolled by.
Then Cleo heard a rabbit and a mole talking.
"Where's the new sheriff?" the rabbit asked.
The mole shrugged.
"This telegram just says the new sheriff will arrive today.
It doesn't say who it is."
Now, to a sneaky cat, this was some mighty good luck.
Cleo had to pinch herself to stop from laughing.
"First, I stole Roscoe's ticket," she thought.
"Now, I'll steal his job!"
Cleo walked right up to that rabbit and mole.
"Hello. I'm Cleo—your new sheriff!"
They tipped their hats.
"Howdy," the rabbit said.
"I'm Mayor Wayne, and this is Fritzy.
He runs our local newspaper, the [i@Prickly Pear Times@i]."
"We're glad you're here," Fritzy said.
Cleo followed the mayor and Fritzy to the sheriff's office.
It was a small building.
Dust covered everything.
"Sorry about the mess," Mayor Wayne said.
"The last sheriff left a while ago."
"He sure was in a hurry," Fritzy said.
"Ah-choo." Cleo sneezed.
"I've been in jails that were nicer than this."
The mayor and Fritzy gave her a funny look.
Cleo pretended to laugh.
"I mean, I've [i@worked@i] in jails that were nicer than this.
But it's fine! I'll clean it up."
"We know the place is humble," Mayor Wayne said.
"But we're humble folks here."
He reached into his coat pocket.
"Here's your badge.
And these are the keys to the doors and jail cells.
Oh, and here are some handcuffs and your slingshot."
Cleo could hardly believe it.
She was the sheriff—with a badge and a slingshot.
And best of all, Prickly Pear seemed peaceful.
Cleo wouldn’t have to do a thing.
"I'm probably the only criminal here," Cleo thought.
"Maybe I'll even like this town."
"We'll let you get settled in," Mayor Wayne said.
"Thanks for taking the job."
Cleo smiled. "It's no problem at all."
"Finally!" Fritzy grinned.
"We have someone to stop the Calamity Gang."
Cleo gulped.
"The Calamity Gang?"
It's a good thing cats have nine lives.
Because the kitty from the city was in deep trouble!
"The Calamity Gang?" Cleo said.
"Are they outlaws?"
Fritzy bit his lip.
"The meanest outlaws in the West!"
Mayor Wayne nodded.
"They're the reason we needed a new sheriff."
It seemed like Cleo's good luck had run out.
"I can't stop a gang of outlaws!" she thought.
She looked at Mayor Wayne and Fritzy.
"But I can't tell them that."
Cleo puffed out her chest. "You can count on me."
"Glad to hear it," Mayor Wayne said.
He and Fritzy left.
"I need to get out of this town!" Cleo thought.
"There must be some money around."
She looked through every drawer and cabinet.
All she found was an old boot.
Cleo sighed.
"Maybe someone in this town has money I can steal."
She opened the front door.
A young owl stood in her way.
"Howdy, miss! I'm Oswald!
Are you the new sheriff?"
"I sure am, kid," Cleo said.
"But I'm busy right now.
I need to check out the town."
"Great!" Oswald said.
"I'll show you around."
Oswald showed Cleo almost every building in town.
That kid sure could talk.
But Cleo wasn't paying much attention.
She was too busy looking at everyone.
"I have to find someone with money," she thought.
"But nobody here looks rich."
"Here we are," Oswald said.
"The Prickly Pear Saloon!"
Cleo and Oswald went inside and sat down.
A badger named Buster poured two glasses of cactus juice.
Cleo took out her coins.
"Oops," she thought.
It wasn't enough to pay for the juice.
"I'm sorry," she said. "But I don't have—"
"I'll pay for that," someone said.
Cleo looked up.
A fox stood nearby.
She wore a long dress with a torn hem.
"Miss Annie!" Oswald grinned.
"Sheriff Cleo, Miss Annie is my teacher!"
Annie smiled. "You must be our new sheriff."
"My name's Cleo. But you don't have to—"
Annie held up a paw.
"In Prickly Pear we help each other out."
Cleo couldn't believe it.
"Annie seems poor," she thought.
"But she's helping me anyway."
Early the next morning, the train chugged along.
Roscoe couldn't sleep.
He was still mad.
"If I ever see Cleo again, I'll throw her in jail!" he thought.
"She's the worst—"
"Hee-ya!"
Roscoe looked out the window.
Riders on horseback raced alongside the train.
"Oh no!" Roscoe said. "Bandits!"
Cleo was asleep at her desk.
Mayor Wayne shook her awake.
"Wake up, Sheriff! The Calamity Gang is attacking the train.
You need to stop them!"
"Huh?" Cleo said.
The mayor led her outside.
Cleo blinked.
A group of townsfolk stared at her.
Their faces were full of hope.
"You'll stop the Calamity Gang, right, Sheriff?" Oswald said.
Cleo gulped and climbed onto her horse. "Sure, kid."
Then she thought, "I'll ride away and never come back."
As she left town, everyone cheered.
"Hooray for Sheriff Cleo!"
"They think I'm a hero," Cleo thought.
"But I'm just a stray from the city. So, how . . ."
Cleo thought of Annie's kindness.
Cleo made a fist. "I'll stop those outlaws!"
[i@Screech!@i] Roscoe felt the train stop suddenly.
An outlaw burst into the car.
"It's Mad Dog Bell!" a passenger yelled.
Roscoe stood up.
Mad Dog drew his slingshot. "Don’t move!"
Three more bandits entered the car.
Mad Dog's eyes narrowed. "No one's going anywhere."
Cleo saw the train stop.
She heard shouts.
"I must be crazy," she thought, galloping toward the train.
"But if I don't stop the Calamity Gang, who will?"
Mad Dog snarled at the passengers.
"Everyone, hand over your wallets and purses."
Roscoe reached for his slingshot.
One outlaw pointed.
"Look out, Boss! He's got a slingshot!"
Mad Dog stepped toward Roscoe.
"I'll take that too!"
It was four against one.
But Roscoe was tough—and smart.
He held up a paw.
"Okay, I'll hand it over. Don't hurt me!"
Roscoe held his slingshot out.
Mad Dog reached for it.
Then Roscoe threw it in his face.
"Ouch!"
Roscoe quickly grabbed his slingshot and loaded a pebble. [i@Fwap!@i]
The other outlaws aimed their slingshots.
Cleo approached the train.
[i@Fwap! Fwap!@i] Slingshots fired inside one of the passenger cars.
Cleo heard shouts.
"The train's being robbed!"
"Help!"
Cleo was scared, but she had to do something.
"Those passengers are counting on me," she thought.
Just then an outlaw flew from the train.
"That dog is tough!"
Cleo pounced on him.
"You're under arrest," she said, slapping handcuffs on the outlaw.
"That wasn't hard," Cleo thought.
"I can do this."
She took a deep breath and jumped into the train. "Whoa!"
Roscoe stood over three other outlaws.
They were tied up.
He glared at her. "What are [i@you@i] doing here?"
Cleo laughed nervously.
"Um, howdy, Roscoe. I'm the new sheriff."
Roscoe couldn't believe it!
Cleo was Prickly Pear's new sheriff?
She was a thief!
She wasn't fit to wear a badge!
"It's not right," he thought.
Roscoe brought the Calamity Gang into town.
Cleo was right behind him.
Several folks stood outside town hall.
"Who's in charge here?" Roscoe asked.
"I'm Mayor Wayne," a rabbit said. "Who are you?"
"I'm Roscoe, your new sheriff."
He nodded toward the outlaws.
"I just caught the Calamity Gang."
"Well, um, thanks," Mayor Wayne said.
"But Cleo is—"
"A thief!" Roscoe said.
"She stole my train ticket—and my job."
More folks began to gather.
Mayor Wayne looked at Cleo. "Is that true?"
"Well, sort of," Cleo said.
"But I did help catch the Calamity Gang."
Roscoe folded his arms.
"She belongs in jail too."
He saw a pretty fox step out of the crowd.
"You should be ashamed—saying mean things!
Maybe Cleo was a thief.
But she's trying to be good now!"
Cleo smiled. "Thanks, Annie."
Roscoe tipped his hat.
"Sorry, miss. But I'm telling the truth."
"Mayor!" a young owl said.
"Cleo is still our sheriff, right?"
The mayor bit his lip.
"I don't know. I . . . um . . ."
"You need to decide, Mayor!" someone shouted.
The mayor scratched his head.
"I know, I know. It's just . . ."
"Let's have a contest!" Cleo said.
"The winner will be the new sheriff."
The mayor looked relieved. "Great idea!"
The next morning everyone gathered outside town hall again.
"The contest will have three rounds," Fritzy said.
"Round one is a quiz."
He opened a law book.
"Cleo, Mr. Dooley let his cows graze in Mrs. Wang's field.
Now it's covered in cow patties.
What do you do?"
Cleo shrugged. "Put the cows in jail?"
"Nope," Fritzy said. "Roscoe?"
"Tell Mr. Dooley to clean up the field," Roscoe said.
"Correct!"
The round went on.
Roscoe got every answer right.
"I won that round," he thought.
"It looks like I'll be the new sheriff!"
"Round two," Fritzy said.
"Shooting slingshots!"
Roscoe went first.
His horse ran fast.
He aimed his slingshot. [i@Fwap! Fwap!@i]
He knocked two cans off a cactus.
The crowd clapped.
Cleo took off. [i@Fwap! Fwap!@i]
She knocked two cans off a cactus with her slingshot.
Then she leaned off the side of her horse.
She grabbed a rock and threw it with her tail.
[i@Ping!@i] A third can went down.
The crowd cheered.
"Cleo wins round two," Fritzy said.
Roscoe felt ill. "I can't let Cleo win!"
Cleo watched the sun set behind the hills.
The final round of the contest was about to begin.
She and Roscoe were tied.
"A good sheriff can track down outlaws," Fritzy said.
"Our friend Zeke is pretending to be an outlaw.
He's hiding in those hills.
Whoever finds him is our new sheriff."
"Can we do this tomorrow?" Cleo asked.
"It's getting dark."
Roscoe snorted. "Sheriffs work whenever they have to."
"Right," Cleo said. "I was just kidding!"
She gulped. "Roscoe is going to win," she thought.
"And I'll go to jail!"
Roscoe and Cleo rode out of town.
Roscoe felt a knot in his belly.
What if Cleo won?
The folks in Prickly Pear seemed to like her.
But it wasn't right!
That cat was a thief!
Roscoe kept looking at the ground.
Cleo gave him a funny look.
"Why are you looking down?"
"I'm looking for tracks," he said.
"Oh," Cleo said. "That's a good idea."
"Mm-hmm," Roscoe snapped.
"That's why I'm the real sheriff."
They rode for a bit longer.
Then Cleo gasped.
"Hoofprints! Lots of them!
So long, Roscoe! Ha-ha!"
She took off.
Roscoe looked at the tracks.
"Those are from several horses," he thought.
"But Zeke probably has only one horse."
He soon found another set of hoofprints.
They were from one horse.
He followed them up a hill.
"Ugh." Cleo stopped near a tree stump.
"I don't see any more tracks.
But I can't turn back.
I have to find Zeke.
If I don't, I'll go to jail."
She found a trail and followed it.
The trail went on and on.
Soon she saw a tree stump.
Cleo groaned. "It's the same one!
I'm going in circles!" She took a breath.
"Maybe I should head back to town.
I'm never going to . . ."
Just then a campfire flickered on a nearby hilltop.
Cleo grinned. "That must be Zeke!"
Roscoe stopped his horse and sniffed.
"Someone's cooking," he thought. "It must be Zeke!"
He followed the scent.
Soon he saw a campfire on a hilltop.
Roscoe rode up to the site.
A toad was cooking beans.
"You found me," the toad said. "I'm Zeke."
"Phew." Roscoe sighed with relief.
"And I'm the sheriff!"
Cleo rode fast.
She could smell the campfire.
"It looks like I'll be the sheriff." She laughed.
"Maybe I can put Roscoe in jail! Ha-ha!"
She reached the hilltop.
Then she stopped laughing.
Three nasty-looking wolves were aiming slingshots at her!
One wolf lowered his slingshot. "Cleo?"
"Tony!" Cleo looked at the other two.
"Tilly! Rupert!"
She couldn't believe her bad luck.
Cleo knew these wolves from the city.
She used to be in their gang.
Nearby she saw sacks of money.
"What are you doing out west?" Cleo asked.
Rupert giggled. "We're robbing banks out here."
"Don't tell Cleo that!" Tony snapped.
"Remember what she did?"
Cleo sure remembered.
She ran away while those wolves robbed a bank in the city.
Tilly glared at her.
"You took off in our getaway wagon.
We were stuck there and got arrested because of you."
"You hurt a customer," Cleo said.
"So I . . . quit."
Tony raised an eyebrow. "What do you do now?"
Cleo gulped. "Um . . ."
Roscoe and Zeke were riding back to town.
Roscoe saw the hoofprints that Cleo followed.
He halted his horse and looked at Zeke.
"Cleo is a city cat.
She could be lost.
We should probably look for her."
They followed the prints.
Soon they saw a campfire.
They got off their horses and sneaked closer.
Cleo was with three wolves—and sacks of money!
"I was right," Roscoe thought. "She's still a thief!"
"You're all under arrest!" Roscoe shouted.
"Including you, Cleo!"
Cleo gasped. "I didn't steal anything!
I'm trying to be the sheriff!"
"Sheriff?" Tony growled.
"I knew we couldn't trust her!"
The wolves drew their slingshots. [i@Fwap! Fwap!@i]
Pebbles flew.
Zeke ran off.
Cleo hid behind a tree.
Roscoe ducked behind a boulder.
Pebbles zinged into Cleo's tree.
Branches snapped off.
Cleo bit her lip. "Maybe I shouldn't be the sheriff!"
She jumped out and ran.
"Get her!" Tony shouted.
Cleo heard Rupert and Tilly behind her.
She ran faster.
Soon she lost them.
She sat down to catch her breath.
"I usually run from the police," she thought.
"Now I'm running from bad guys too!" She sighed.
"Maybe I should stop running."
Roscoe watched the two outlaws chase Cleo.
The dog was starting to wonder if he was wrong.
"Maybe Cleo isn't friends with the wolves," he thought.
"That means she's in danger because of me."
Another pebble bounced off the boulder.
"I know you're there!" Tony shouted.
"You can't hide forever!"
Roscoe leaped up and shot a pebble. [i@Fwap!@i]
He ducked back down as another pebble flew toward him.
"This is bad," Roscoe thought.
"I'm stuck behind this boulder, and Cleo is in danger!"
Just then he heard something.
Someone was coming!
Roscoe aimed his slingshot.
Then he saw a familiar figure.
"Cleo!" Roscoe whispered. "You came back!"
Cleo nodded. "I want to help!"
By now Roscoe was sure that Cleo wasn't working with the wolves.
But this was a mighty dangerous situation.
He shook his head.
"You're not a cop, Cleo.
This is too dangerous for you."
Another pebble whizzed past them.
"It's too dangerous for anyone," Cleo said.
"Besides, I used to, um, know these wolves. I can help!"
Roscoe heard footsteps.
The other wolves were back.
"Did you find Cleo?" Tony asked.
"No," Tilly said.
Rupert giggled.
"But we got the toad!"
Roscoe peeked out.
Poor Zeke was tied up!
"Cleo!" Roscoe whispered.
"You're good at sneaking, right?"
Cleo grinned. "I'm the best."
Roscoe nodded. "And I know you're a good pickpocket."
He quickly told Cleo his plan.
Then Cleo crawled in one direction while Roscoe crawled in the other.
A few minutes later, Roscoe stood behind a tree.
He held one end of a rope.
"I hope this works," he thought.
He took a deep breath and started shouting.
"Cleo, help! I'm hurt—I can't walk!"
Cleo slipped to the other side of the campsite.
She heard Roscoe shout for help.
Tony laughed. "That dog is hurt!
This is our chance to get him!" He ran off.
Cleo crawled to Zeke and untied him.
Then she crept closer to Tilly and Rupert.
She reached out and plucked the slingshots from their belts.
They didn't even feel it!
"Help!" Tony shouted.
Rupert and Tilly ran to him.
Cleo followed.
She saw Tony hanging from a tree, a rope around his foot.
Tilly and Rupert reached for their slingshots.
"Ahem." Cleo held up their slingshots. "Looking for these?"
Roscoe quickly tied up Tilly and Rupert.
"You won, Roscoe," Cleo said.
"You're the sheriff. Are you still going to . . ."
"Put you in jail?" Roscoe asked.
"No. Stay out of trouble, though, okay?"
Cleo nodded. "Sure thing, Sheriff."
The next morning federal marshals came for the Calamity Gang.
They took the wolves away too.
Roscoe sat at his desk and smiled.
"Now I'll have some peace and quiet," he thought.
"No more Calamity Gang and no more—"
The door flew open, and Cleo walked in.
Roscoe jumped up. "What are you doing here?"
Cleo showed him a badge, grinning.
"Everyone here likes me, Roscoe.
They made me your deputy!"
An ice delivery was on its way to Prickly Pear.
And thank goodness! That sun was blazing!
Folks gathered at the train station to wait for the special delivery.
"It sure is hot," Roscoe said.
Cleo nodded. "I can't wait to get some cold cactus juice."
When the train arrived, two workers unloaded blocks of ice.
The blocks were covered in sawdust.
"What's the sawdust for?" Cleo asked.
"It keeps the ice from melting," Sam said.
A worker placed an ice block in Sam's wheelbarrow.
The crow hurried back to his general store.
The workers lifted another block of ice.
Some of the sawdust fell off.
Fritzy pointed. "Something's inside that ice!"
Folks crowded around to see.
The workers cut into the ice.
Finally it split apart.
"It's a sack," Annie said.
Mayor Wayne scratched his head.
"What's a sack doing inside a block of ice?"
The ice workers opened the sack.
Zeke gasped. "It's full of gold bars!"
The workers jumped up and down.
"We're rich, Emmett!"
"We sure are, Bucky!"
"Hold on," Roscoe said.
"This gold belongs to someone else."
Emmett frowned. "Who are you?"
Roscoe pointed to his badge. "I'm the sheriff of Prickly Pear."
"And I'm the deputy," Cleo said.
"Well, we found the gold," Bucky said.
"That means it's ours."
"What about all of us?" Buster asked.
"After all, we bought the ice!"
"That's a good point," Zeke said.
"Right, Mayor?"
Mayor Wayne bit his lip. "Um, I suppose . . ."
"Folks!" Roscoe said.
"The law says we can't just keep the gold.
We must give the owner time to claim it."
He closed the sack.
After that, most folks grew quiet.
But the workers looked at each other.
"What if the owner doesn't claim it?" Emmett asked.
"Then we can share it," Roscoe said. "All of us."
Folks suddenly started talking again.
They liked the idea of sharing all that gold.
The only ones who didn't look happy were Emmett and Bucky.
"Deputy Cleo and I will take the sack for now," Roscoe said.
"We'll keep it safe at the sheriff's office."
"That's right, folks." Cleo grinned.
"For now, it belongs to me and the sheriff."
Roscoe frowned. "It doesn't belong to us, Deputy.
We're just keeping it safe."
He turned to the crowd.
"Don't get your hopes up.
Someone will probably come to claim this gold."
"But if they don't, it's ours!" Zeke said.
The crowd cheered.
Roscoe sighed.
Everyone in Prickly Pear was excited about that gold.
But Sheriff Roscoe was just thinking about his job.
He turned to Cleo. "Can you send a telegram to the newspapers?
They can print a notice about the gold.
I'll go and lock up the sack."
"Sure," Cleo said.
In the sheriff's office, Roscoe put the sack inside the safe.
"I'll set a new code for the combination lock," he thought.
"I'll use numbers that I won't forget."
He carefully turned the dial to different numbers.
"Thirty-six, five, seventeen." Roscoe shut the safe. [i@Click!@i]
He went outside.
Cleo was helping a farmer remove a wheel from his wagon.
The wheel was broken.
It was also stuck.
The farmer hit the wheel with a hammer to loosen it.
Roscoe and Cleo pulled.
Finally the wheel popped off.
"Thanks!" the farmer said.
"I hope the repair shop has a 40-inch wheel."
Cleo turned to Roscoe.
"Alright, Sheriff. Let's send that—"
"Oh no!" someone shouted.
"That came from the stable!" Roscoe said.
He and Cleo ran to the stable.
Jake, the stable owner, was upset.
"I just got back from breakfast.
Two horses are missing!"
Roscoe and Cleo searched everywhere.
But the dirt was covered with too many hoofprints.
After a couple of hours, they gave up.
Roscoe sighed. "Maybe the horses will come back on their own.
Let's send that telegram now."
Fritzy sat down at his telegraph machine.
"What should the telegram say, Sheriff?"
"'A sack was found in Prickly Pear,'" Roscoe said.
"'Its contents are valuable.'"
Fritzy tapped on the telegraph machine, but nothing happened.
"Hmm," he said.
"The machine isn't working. We need to check the line."
They followed the telegraph line outside of town.
Roscoe and Cleo rode alongside Fritzy's wagon.
Around noon they spotted a wire hanging down from a pole.
Everyone stopped.
"Some of the wires are old," Fritzy said.
"They wear out and then break."
He ran around to a spool of new wire.
"We'll need 16 feet of wire."
Roscoe walked backward, unwinding the wire.
Cleo watched as the wire came off the spool.
"Three feet . . . four feet . . . five feet . . ."
Fritzy unloaded his toolbox.
"Fifteen . . . ," Cleo said as the wire came off the spool.
"And . . . 16 feet! Stop!"
Fritzy gasped. He was looking at the old wire.
"This wire isn't worn out."
Cleo scratched her head. "What does that mean?"
Fritzy frowned. "It means someone cut it to stop us from sending that telegram."
Roscoe nodded. "And it could be anyone in town!"
It was hot work repairing that telegraph line.
The job took all afternoon.
Fritzy sent the telegram that evening.
In the morning Roscoe and Cleo got ready to interview townsfolk.
They needed to find out who cut the wire.
"Never rush an interview," Roscoe said.
"Get folks to trust you first. Then they'll start talking."
"Got it," Cleo said.
They started with Zeke.
"You're not in trouble," Roscoe said.
"We just need to know where you were yesterday."
"After the ice arrived," Cleo added.
"I was in the hills," Zeke said, "panning for gold."
"What time?" Roscoe asked.
Zeke rubbed his chin. "From eight thirty to six."
Roscoe wrote that down. "Eight thirty to six."
He looked back at Zeke.
"You seemed excited about the gold in that sack."
"Sure!" Zeke said. "Everyone's excited about it."
Cleo rolled her eyes. This was taking forever!
"Did you cut the telegraph wire?" Cleo snapped.
Zeke gasped. "No!"
Roscoe gave her a dirty look.
Next they met with Mayor Wayne.
"Sorry, Mayor," Roscoe said.
"But I have to ask.
Where were you yesterday after the ice delivery?"
"Let's see," the mayor said.
"I got to my office at 8:20 or maybe 8:50.
I had three meetings. Or was it four?"
Roscoe wrote this down. "Eight twenty . . . eight fifty . . . three or four meetings."
Cleo yawned. Then she stood up.
"Did you cut the telegraph wire?"
Mayor Wayne snorted. "Of course not!"
Roscoe headed to the schoolhouse with Cleo.
He felt bad enough about interviewing everyone.
His deputy was making things even worse.
"This time I'll ask all the questions," Roscoe said.
"You don't have the skills it takes yet."
"Hmph!" Cleo frowned. "I have plenty of skills."
Annie was at the chalkboard.
Roscoe saw math problems all over it.
"Howdy!" Oswald waved.
"Good afternoon, Sheriff," Annie said.
